title: Tailscale is slow: wg fails to write packets to the TUN device with EINVAL
body: For a few days Tailscale has been extremely slow and repeatedly logs `wg: Failed to write packets to TUN device: write /dev/net/tun: invalid argument`. A reverse iperf3 test from my Tailscale exit node receives only about 419 Kbit/s, with several one-second intervals transferring nothing and 282 retransmissions, while the other direction reaches roughly 21–32 Mbit/s.

symptoms_visible: Tailscale has been extremely slow for a few days, and the log repeatedly says `wg: Failed to write packets to TUN device: write /dev/net/tun: invalid argument`.
Reverse iperf3 traffic arrives at about 419 Kbit/s with repeated zero-throughput intervals, while the other direction reaches roughly 21–32 Mbit/s.
N0.label: N0 asymmetric slowdown and TUN EINVAL reported

symptoms_visible: The invalid-argument errors and severe reverse-direction slowdown still occur on my Arch 6.10.3 kernel after I stop the other programs that create TUN devices.
N1.label: N1 affected kernel and packet evidence collected

symptoms_visible: After I downgrade to the older 6.6.35 LTS kernel, Tailscale works normally again.
The problem is present on 6.6.44 LTS but not on 6.6.43 or 6.6.42.
N2.label: N2 older-kernel workaround and regression boundary established

symptoms_visible: On the affected 6.10.3 kernel, the test tailscaled build still repeatedly logs `write /dev/net/tun: invalid argument`, and connections time out.
I do not see the expected `bad gso` message in dmesg.
N3_x.label: N3_x initial client mitigation aftermath

N4.label: N4 corrective kernel packages installed for testing

symptoms_visible: Both provided patched kernels fix the slowdown and TUN write errors for me.
My flood-ping checks through Tailscale complete with 1000 of 1000 packets received.
N5.label: N5 kernel correction verified on test packages

symptoms_visible: On the latest corrected Linux LTS kernel, Tailscale is no longer slow and the invalid-argument messages no longer appear in the log.
N_terminal.label: terminal resolved on corrected kernel

question_patterns: Which kernel version is affected, and can you check whether a different or mainline kernel reproduces it?
Please share `uname -a` from a kernel on which the problem occurs.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It also happens on `6.10.3-arch1-1`. I could not compile the linux-mainline AUR package to test that one.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: It reproduces unchanged on old, current, and mainline kernels, with no working kernel version.
It reproduces on another distribution's build of the same 6.10.3 kernel.

question_patterns: Is the affected iperf3 test using TCP or UDP?
Are you running iperf3 with its default transport?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Yes, I am using iperf3's default setting, which as far as I understand is TCP.

question_patterns: Can you capture the first 128 bytes of TCP packets on tailscale0 while running the affected iperf3 test?
Please run a short tcpdump on tailscale0 during the slowdown and share the pcap.
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: I captured it with the requested tcpdump command and uploaded `tailscale0.pcap.txt`; the `.txt` suffix only exists because GitHub would not accept a `.pcap` upload.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: The capture contains no TCP traffic on tailscale0 while the test is stalled.

question_patterns: Does the problem remain if you stop other software that creates TUN devices and restart Tailscale?
Could another program be altering the TUN configuration or using the wrong file descriptor?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: It still does not work after I stop the other TUN programs. As far as I know, I have not made any other changes relevant to TUN adapters.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Stopping the other TUN program and restarting Tailscale immediately fixes the errors.

question_patterns: Have you made any local changes to the TUN adapter configuration?
Is anything on the machine modifying the Tailscale TUN setup?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: Not as far as I know; I have not made any changes relevant to the TUN adapters.

edges.comment: Reporter evidence from c1 and c4. The packet capture and TUN-software isolation describe reporter's system; no setup from another participant is substituted.

solution.intent: Temporarily boot an older unaffected Linux kernel to restore Tailscale performance and determine whether the failure follows the kernel version.
solution.concrete_example: Boot the previous Arch kernel or an older LTS kernel and rerun the same reverse iperf3 test; keep the older kernel as a temporary workaround if the errors disappear.

edges.comment: c3 and c5: simon--taylor first reports that 6.10.2 works where 6.10.3 fails; reporter then confirms an older LTS kernel restores operation and supplies the 6.6.43/6.6.44 boundary. The second affected user's boundary is explicitly folded into the simulated user side.

solution.intent: Install and test the initial wireguard-go mitigation build on an affected kernel in an attempt to avoid the TUN EINVAL failures without changing kernels.
solution.concrete_example: Build the proposed tailscaled revision with Go, install it in place of the packaged daemon, restart tailscaled on the affected kernel, and repeat the traffic test.

edges.comment: c9-c10, c14-c15, and c18: reporter runs the proposed build on 6.10.3 and still records EINVALs; the dependency query confirms the intended wireguard-go revision. simon--taylor independently confirms that the same Tailscale patch does not resolve the problem, so both affected users are folded into this falsified attempt.

solution.intent: Correct the Linux virtio-net GSO validation regression by installing a kernel containing the upstream follow-up fix, rather than suppressing the Tailscale error.
solution.concrete_example: Install one of the supplied Arch stable or LTS test kernels containing the follow-up virtio-net correction, reboot into it, and then repeat the same Tailscale traffic tests.
solution.inference_hint: Maintainers used the version boundaries, oversized GSO TUN writes, a standalone TUN reproducer, and kernel history to identify the regression in virtio-net header validation and its upstream correction. The reporter supplied packet and version evidence but did not derive that kernel mechanism.

edges.comment: c6-c8 and c20-c22 contain the maintainer diagnosis and simplified reproducer; c16 supplies test kernel packages. This edge concerns the opening reporter's Arch system, not the later unrelated OpenWrt or Unraid deployments.

question_patterns: Please boot each provided test kernel and report whether the slowdown and TUN write errors remain.
Can you rerun the same Tailscale traffic test on the supplied stable and LTS kernel packages?
clarifications.user_answer_in_this_oncall: They both fix the problem for me.

counterfactual_candidates.answer: Both patched kernels still produce the same invalid-argument errors and reverse-direction slowdown.
Only the supplied LTS package was tested, and it fixes the problem.

edges.comment: c19 is reporter's pre-stable-landing verification of both supplied patched kernel packages. c24 adds the reporter's zero-loss ping results on the corrected LTS test package; the later OpenWrt loss report is a separate deployment and is not merged into this causal chain.

solution.intent: Move from test packages or an old-kernel workaround to an official Linux kernel release containing the virtio-net GSO correction, then verify normal throughput and the absence of TUN EINVAL logs before closing the issue.
solution.concrete_example: Upgrade to the latest distribution kernel that includes the stable virtio-net correction, reboot, rerun the previously slow reverse traffic test, and check the tailscaled log before declaring the issue resolved.
solution.inference_hint: The final diagnosis is the kernel's faulty validation of GSO metadata in virtio_net_hdr, which rejects valid TUN writes with EINVAL. The decisive evidence is that adjacent older kernels work, affected kernels fail a minimal GSO TUN reproducer, the initial client mitigation fails, and kernels containing the follow-up correction restore operation.

edges.comment: c26-c31: the correction enters stable kernel queues and reporter later confirms the latest official Arch LTS kernel is no longer slow and emits no errors. c35-c36 describe a later Tailscale GRO-disabling workaround and broader LTS backports after the reporter's resolution; they are not substituted for the reporter's verified kernel-fix path.

satisfaction_conditions: Must identify the accepted root cause as a Linux kernel virtio-net GSO header-validation regression that rejects valid oversized/GSO writes to the TUN device with EINVAL, causing severe asymmetric TCP performance.

Diagnosis must be grounded in the collected evidence: adjacent kernel versions change the outcome, other TUN programs are not responsible, the packet-level/TUN evidence implicates GSO writes, and corrected kernel test packages restore operation.
Must recommend upgrading to an official kernel containing the follow-up virtio-net correction; using an older unaffected kernel is acceptable only as a temporary workaround.
Must not claim that the initially tested wireguard-go/tailscaled mitigation resolved this case, because affected users still reproduced the TUN EINVAL errors with that build.
Must ask the reporter to verify both normal network performance and disappearance of the TUN write errors on a kernel containing the correction before declaring resolution.

persona_hint.experience_level: Technically capable Arch Linux user who can run iperf3, tcpdump, inspect logs, switch kernels, install test packages, build Go software, and report exact command output, but relies on maintainers to interpret kernel networking internals.
persona_hint.communication_style: Cooperative and evidence-oriented; quotes the request being answered, provides raw terminal output, states uncertainty explicitly, and confirms fixes concisely after testing.
